articles.title: Rs 6.86 crore Mumbai flat in Lower Parel sold for Rs 5.36 crore, Rs 5 crore adjusted as brokerage; Lodha Developers alleges Rs 6.67 crore loss in Mankoli land acquisition and Lower Parel flat deal; files third case against former director Rajendra Lodha
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Lodha Developers Ltd has lodged a fresh complaint against its former director, business development officer Shivaji Jadhav and others, alleging
articles.body: MUMBAI: Lodha Developers Ltd has lodged a fresh complaint against its former director, business development officer Shivaji Jadhav and others, alleging that they caused a financial loss of Rs 6.67 crore to the company through irregularities in a land acquisition deal at Mankoli in Bhiwandi, Thane district, and a related flat transaction in Lower Parel.This is the third case registered against Rajendra Lodha.The company lodged an FIR with the NM Joshi Marg police, which has since been transferred to the city crime branch. The alleged irregularities involved a purported Rs 5 crore brokerage agreement, a Rs 1.5 crore discount on a luxury apartment and payments made in connection with the acquisition of 6,420 square metres of land.The land in question is located in Mankoli village. The company entered into a development agreement with Chandrasen Bhoir and his family in January 2019. Under the agreement, the landowners were to receive 24,075 square feet of saleable built-up area in exchange for the agricultural land.Subsequently, Avinash Bhoir claimed possession of a portion of the land, following which the company entered into a supplementary agreement to provide him with 1,425 square feet of saleable built-up area. Nitin Keni also claimed possession of land covered by the three survey numbers. According to the complaint, the company entered into a supplementary agreement with Keni on May 4, 2019, and paid him Rs 17 lakh in connection with his claim.The complaint alleges that Haridas Bhoir acted as a broker in the original land transaction and received Rs 8.5 lakh. However, the company subsequently discovered alleged irregularities involving Sackveer Builds and Developers LLP, whose representatives, Sachin K Dhaktode and Virji K Dhadi, had purchased Flat No. B-5802 at Lodha Alura, Lodha Park, Lower Parel.According to the complaint, the flat was originally priced at Rs 6.86 crore. On the recommendation of then director Rajendra Lodha, its price was allegedly reduced by around Rs 1.5 crore, and the property was sold for approximately Rs 5.36 crore. The flat was registered on July 19, 2019.The complaint further alleges that an inter-office note dated July 30, 2019, signed by Rajendra Lodha and Shivaji Jadhav, directed that Rs 5 crore be adjusted against the flat's purchase price, purportedly towards brokerage for the Mankoli land transaction.A brokerage agreement was subsequently executed on July 31, 2019, between Sackveer Builds and Developers LLP and Lodha Developers Pvt Ltd. The agreement, signed on behalf of the company by Babusingh Rajguru, allegedly provided for a payment of ₹5 crore for making the land title clear and marketable. An affidavit submitted by the developers' representatives also referred to the payment.However, an internal investigation allegedly found that Sackveer Builds and Developers LLP had no involvement in the acquisition of the Mankoli land. The company further claimed that neither the brokerage agreement nor the inter-office note could be found in its records during the review of the transactions.The complaint alleges that Rajendra Lodha, Shivaji Jadhav, Babusingh Rajguru and others misused the authority entrusted to them and conspired to route the alleged brokerage amount through the flat transaction. The FIR names six individuals in connection with the alleged Rs 6.67 crore loss, comprising the Rs 5 crore brokerage adjustment, the Rs 1.5 crore discount and the Rs 17 lakh payment to Keni.Interestingly, the original complaint submitted to the police did not name Rajendra Lodha. articles.title: Nithya Raman wins LA mayoral race, becoming city’s first South Asian mayor
articles.summary: DSA-backed Raman will lead the second-largest US city, promising action on homelessness and affordable housing.
articles.body:
Nithya Raman, a progressive Los Angeles City Council member, has defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, putting her on track to become the first South Asian to lead the second-largest city in the United States.

The Associated Press called the race for Raman on Thursday, with Raman holding 52 percent of the vote.

Raman, 45, overtook Bass despite the incumbent’s support from prominent Democrats such as California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

Her campaign was backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), with her victory coming as part of a surge in visibility and electoral wins for the left-wing political movement.

A record number of candidates backed or affiliated with the DSA won federal offices in Tuesday’s midterm elections. On its website, the DSA has claimed credit for contributing to at least 300 candidacies or ballot referendums during the midterms, and it said it is on track to count 105 of those as victories.

Some of those wins came in congressional races, with figures such as Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez, Melat Kiros and Chris Rabb winning their first terms as US representatives.

Raman’s victory in Los Angeles follows another high-profile democratic socialist winning a mayor’s race in New York City last year: Zohran Mamdani.

Raman was born in India and worked as an urban planner before running for office. Once an ally of Bass, she had initially endorsed her re-election campaign but reversed course, entering the mayoral race in February, just hours before the filing deadline.

In her victory speech, Raman promised to restore what she called an ambitious, creative and entrepreneurial Los Angeles.

“For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do,” she told the crowd.

Raman also pledged to expand affordable housing, improve neglected city services and take a different approach to homelessness by deploying more medical teams to assist people who are unhoused.

In addition, she called for replacing the city’s police chief over concerns about cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Raman now faces the task of delivering on those promises in a city of more than 3.8 million people.

Los Angeles also faces the challenge of hosting the 2028 Olympic Games, which open in July of that year.

With the result, Bass has become the first Los Angeles mayor in more than two decades to lose a re-election bid.

Her defeat follows a difficult four years in office. Her administration faced mounting criticism over the city’s homelessness crisis and its response to the deadly Palisades Fire , which broke out while she was overseas and devastated communities across the Los Angeles area.

In a statement on Thursday, Bass congratulated Raman and said she was committed to ensuring a smooth transition.

“Four years ago, you elected me as the first Black woman mayor in the history of Los Angeles. You gave me the honor of serving the city that raised me, and every single day since, I have carried that responsibility with me,” Bass wrote .

“Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”

articles.summary: Imagens de câmera de segurança registraram o momento em que a vítima foi derrubada pela enxurrada no Bairro Grama. Apesar do susto, ela não ficou ferida.
articles.body:
Uma mulher foi arrastada pela correnteza durante o temporal que atingiu Juiz de Fora nesta quinta-feira (5). Um vídeo de câmera de segurança de um estabelecimento comercial mostra o momento em que ela é levada pela força da água na Rua Diomar Monteiro, no Bairro Grama.

Mulher é arrastada por correnteza durante temporal em Juiz de Fora — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

O comerciante Sandro Carlos de Jesus estava no local no momento do ocorrido e conversou com o g1. Ele disse que os alagamentos na região são frequentes e que a água subiu rapidamente.

“Realmente, ali desce muita água. Toda a enxurrada do morro acaba parando nessa esquina. A mulher subiu pelo passeio, mas, quando foi atravessar a rua, a enxurrada a derrubou e a arrastou morro abaixo”, relatou.

Ao perceber a situação, um motorista que passava pelo local parou o veículo para resgatar a mulher, que estava caída. De acordo com Sandro, apesar do susto, ela não ficou ferida.

“Depois disso, ela voltou ao local e está tudo bem. Eu até pedi para ela ir para casa, e ela me ouviu e foi na hora”, disse.

articles.title: Como utilizar a nota do Enem  | G1
articles.standfirst: Provas acontecem dias 8 e 15 de novembro. Mais de 5 milhões de pessoas tiveram a inscrição confirmada e estão aptas a participar da edição de 2026 do exame.
articles.summary: Provas acontecem dias 8 e 15 de novembro.  Mais de 5 milhões de pessoas tiveram a inscrição confirmada e estão aptas a participar da edição de 2026 do exame.
articles.body:
O Enem é a principal porta de entrada para o ensino superior no Brasil, pois permite a seus participantes concorrer a vagas em universidades públicas e privadas, e até a financiamento e bolsas privadas, com as notas obtidas nas provas.

Em 2026, as provas da aplicação regular acontecem nos dias 8 e 15 de novembro. Mais de 5 milhões de pessoas tiveram a inscrição confirmada e estão aptas a participar do exame.

ENEM 2025 - DOMINGO (16) – RIBEIRÃO PRETO (SP) – Caderno de prova laranja no 2º dia de prova — Foto: Érico Andrade/g1

Abaixo, veja os diversos usos possíveis do exame:

Desde 2025, o Enem voltou a servir para certificar de conclusão do ensino médio para maiores de 18 anos. Os critérios para a certificação de conclusão do ensino médio são:

Pontuação mínima em cada área do conhecimento igual ou maior a 450 pontos);

Alcançar pelo menos 500 pontos na redação; e

Ter, no mínimo, 18 anos completos no primeiro dia de prova.

Após receber o resultado do Enem, os interessados deverão se dirigir a uma unidade dos Institutos Federais de Educação, Ciência e Tecnologia ou às instituições estaduais que tenham firmado termo de adesão com o Inep, levando a documentação necessária para solicitar a emissão do certificado.

A prova havia deixado de ter essa função em 2017, por decisão do Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais Anísio Teixeira (Inep). Desde então, adultos que não se formaram na idade correta passaram a buscar o diploma do ensino médio (e também do fundamental) por meio do Exame Nacional para Certificação de Competências de Jovens e Adultos (Encceja).

Universidade Federal do Recôncavo da Bahia (UFRB) de Cruz das Almas — Foto: Luis Fortes/MEC

Para quem quer cursar o ensino superior do Brasil aproveitando o desempenho no exame, há algumas alternativas, tanto do governo federal quanto iniciativas privadas. Confira as principais:

O Sistema de Seleção Unificada (Sisu) é o programa do Ministério da Educação (MEC) que seleciona estudantes para universidades públicas.

Em 2026, as inscrições para o programa aconteceram de19 a 23 de janeiro. Serão 274,8 mil vagas em 7.388 cursos e 136 universidades de todo o país.

Atualmente, o programa tem apenas uma edição por ano. Portanto, a edição única seleciona alunos que vão iniciar o período letivo no primeiro ou no segundo semestre.

Em geral, o Sisu tem uma chamada regular seguida pela lista de espera, para preencher eventuais vagas ociosas.

Pela primeira vez, em 2026, o programa passou a aceitar as notas das três edições mais recentes do Enem . Neste caso, Enem 2023, 2024 e 2025. Até então, podiam se inscrever apenas quem havia feito a última edição do exame.

Como funciona: Na inscrição, é preciso escolher até duas opções de cursos e/ou de instituição. Ao longo do período de inscrição, o candidato pode mudar as opções no sistema quantas vezes quiser, tomando como base as notas de corte parciais divulgadas diariamente. Há vagas para cotistas (as regras variam de instituição para instituição).

Pré-requisitos: ter prestado ao menos uma das três edições mais recentes do Enem e tirado nota superior a zero na redação.

O Programa Universidade para Todos (Prouni) é uma iniciativa do MEC que oferece bolsas integrais (100%) e parciais (50% de desconto) em instituições de ensino particulares.

Como funciona: O candidato deve indicar, em ordem de preferência, até duas opções de curso (selecionando a instituição de ensino e o turno). Depois, é necessário marcar se quer participar na modalidade de ampla concorrência ou de cotas. Por fim, precisa monitorar, a cada dia, a nota parcial para aqueles cursos. Se quiser, pode mudar suas escolhas (valerá a última opção marcada no período de inscrições).

Pré-requisitos: O candidato deve ter feito o Enem em uma das duas últimas edições, ter obtido média mínima de 450 pontos nas áreas de conhecimento e nota superior a zero na redação. É preciso também pertencer a uma família com renda per capita de até 3 salários mínimos e ter ensino médio completo (em escola pública ou particular). Há vagas para pessoas com deficiência e professores da rede pública.

Tipos de bolsa: Integral (renda familiar mensal per capita de até 1,5 salário mínimo) e parcial (que cobre 50% da mensalidade, para renda familiar mensal per capita de 1,5 a 3 salários mínimos).

O Fundo de Financiamento Estudantil (Fies) é um programa do governo federal que paga parte das mensalidades de estudantes em universidades e faculdades privadas, com a contrapartida de os beneficiários quitarem o financiamento após a formatura.

Como funciona: O crédito pode cobrir de 50% a 100% da mensalidade do curso, com juros que dependem da renda familiar do candidato.

Vagas: Em 2025, foram ofertadas 112.168 novas vagas para o Fies. 67.301 delas no primeiro semestre e 44.867 no segundo semestre.

Há instituições privadas de ensino superior que usam a nota do Enem no processo seletivo ou que oferecem descontos nas mensalidades a partir do desempenho do candidato nesse exame. As regras e datas variam de universidade para universidade.

Também há instituições e empresas privadas que oferecem financiamentos particulares para o ensino superior. Neste caso, os prazos, condições de pagamento e juros são definidos diretamente com a empresa responsável.

articles.title: Crise no Paraguai: empresário perde R$ 200 mil com quebra de banco | G1
articles.standfirst: 'Há um clima de forte revolta e raiva direcionado ao presidente e aos políticos do país', relata brasileiro ao g1. Outra entrevistada diz que banco fez campanha dias antes para clientes não tirarem dinheiro.
articles.summary: 'Há um clima de forte revolta e raiva direcionado ao presidente e aos políticos do país', relata brasileiro ao g1. Outra entrevistada diz que banco fez campanha dias antes.
articles.body:
Ueno Bank no Paraguai — Foto: Marcos Landim/RPC

A crise bancária e política que abala o Paraguai nos últimos dias afetou também a vida de brasileiros que moram no país. O g1 conversou com um empresário que perdeu mais de R$ 200 mil, uma cambista que ficou sem o dinheiro que economizou para as férias e um dono de oficina que ficou sem capital de giro.

O Ueno Bank , que tinha cerca de 3 milhões de clientes, aproximadamente 60% da população adulta paraguaia, foi liquidado pelo Banco Central do país, dois dias depois, nesta quinta-feira (5) o presidente Santiago Peña, anúnciou sua renúncia ao cargo.

Segundo estimativas do Itamaraty, cerca de 270 mil brasileiros residem no país que faz fronteira com Mato Grosso do Sul e Paraná.

Crise no Ueno Bank: Na terça-feira (3), o BC paraguaio liquidou o bando digital após constatar que o índice de solvência da instituição havia caído para menos da metade do mínimo exigido por lei. O rombo tem origem em empréstimos concedidos a empresas ligadas ao próprio banco, que comprometeram seus recursos e deixaram milhares de clientes sem acesso ao dinheiro.

Renúncia de Santiago Peña : Dois dias após a intervenção no banco, Santiago Peña, que já foi acionista de empresas ligadas ao grupo controlador do Ueno, anunciou sua renúncia à presidência. A Câmara dos Deputados aprovou por unanimidade o avanço de um processo de impeachment contra o presidente.

Marcelo Bernard, 26 anos, está entre os brasileiros prejudicados. No Paraguai há dois anos e dono de um oficina em Presidente Franco, ao lado a tríplice fronteira, ele perdeu parte de dinheiro que estava no Ueno.

Marcelo perdeu cerca de 5 milhões de guaranis, cerca de R$ 4,5 mil . O prejuízo poderia ser maior se, por lá, não tivesse a cultura de se pagar em notas.

"Para mim a situação não está tão ruim porque no Paraguai as pessoas ainda estão acostumadas a pagar em dinheiro vivo, então eu não tinha todo o meu dinheiro no banco. Eu tinha cerca de 5 milhões de guaranis lá, mas o dinheiro de giro eu mantinha na carteira", disse.

Marcelo ainda conta que o clima por lá é de completa consternação.

"Há um clima de forte revolta e raiva direcionado ao presidente e aos políticos do país. Por ser uma sociedade conservadora e firme, as pessoas exigem punição rigorosa aos responsáveis", contou.

Se por um lado o dono da oficina não teve tanta parte de seu dinheiro atingido, outros brasileiros não tiveram a mesma 'sorte'.

Brasileiro perde mais de R$ 200 mil no banco Ueno

O brasileiro Pedro Treméa, 61 anos, tem uma empresa de refrigeração em Ciudad del Este, também na triplice fronteira. Ele contou que o valor perdido no banco Ueno foi maior do que o valor coberto pelo Fundo de Garantia de Depósitos (FGD), o FGC paraguaio.

➡️ O Fundo de Garantia de Depósitos do Paraguai cobre até 228,3 milhões de guaranis por pessoa e por instituição financeira, o equivalente a aproximadamente R$ 200 mil. O limite corresponde a 75 salários mínimos paraguaios. Quem tinha valores acima desse teto poderá depender do processo de resolução do banco para tentar recuperar o dinheiro.

Cliente do banco desde a época em que a instituição ainda era o Banco Visión, que foi incorporado pelo Ueno em 2021, Pedro utilizava a conta principalmente para movimentar o capital de giro da empresa. No entanto, como o empresário diversificava as instituições em que guardava seu dinheiro, o impacto foi limitado.

"Como empresa, não colocamos todo o recurso em um único banco. No Paraguai é muito utilizado o alias (sistema de transferência instantânea similar ao Pix), e mantemos duas ou três contas em instituições diferentes para atender clientes de várias regiões, o que evitou um impacto ainda pior", contou.

Além do prejuízo e da incereteza de quando vai reaver o dinheiro perdido, Treméa diz que a crise financeira vai afetara diretamente seu negócio, já que importa seus produtos do Brasil e realiza operações em dólares ou reais.

A cotação da moeda americana passou de 5.900 para 6.500 guaranis em apenas 24 horas, em meio à especulação financeira provocada pela crise.

Pedro também contou que todos os funcionários de sua empresa tinham conta no Ueno, atraídos pela facilidade de abertura da conta digital e pela oferta de cartões de crédito. Ele preferiu não especificar o valor que perdeu.

Vista aérea mostra a sede do Ueno Bank, em Assunção, no Paraguai. — Foto: Reuters

Outra brasileira afetada é Dalma Morinigo, de 31 anos, que mora há quatro em Ciudad del Este e trabalha em uma casa de câmbio. Ela tinha o correspondente em guaranis a mais de R$ 7 mil depositados no Ueno , e planejava usar o valor para as férias de fim de ano.

Dalma também utilizava a conta para receber pagamentos de clientes. Ela era correntista do banco havia quase dois anos e diz que escolheu a instituição pela facilidade para abrir uma conta, pela oferta de serviços digitais e pela presença de caixas eletrônicos em diferentes pontos da cidade.

Ela também diz que, dias antes da liquidação, o banco oferecia uma campanha de reembolso de 50% de determinados valores mantidos na conta. Segundo Dalma, a oferta teria incentivado clientes a não retirar o dinheiro.

A brasileira conta que foi surpreendida pela notícia. Ao tentar acessar o aplicativo depois de saber da crise, percebeu que o saldo não aparecia mais e que não conseguia realizar operações.

Print do aplicativo da conta de Dalma no Banco Ueno. — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

"Não há muito a ser feito, temos que esperar. Dizem que até em cinco dias iremos receber, mas não acredito muito nisso", afirmou.

Peña anunciou medidas para ressarcir clientes

Diante da crise, Peña anunciou um acordo com líderes do Congresso para acelerar a votação de um projeto que permite utilizar recursos do Fundo de Garantia do país para ressarcir os clientes do banco.

O presidente afirmou ainda que a medida deve garantir a devolução dos recursos públicos depositados no banco, incluindo valores do IPS e de outros fundos públicos de previdência.

Nesta quarta-feira (4), Peña promulgou a lei que permitirá aos clientes do Ueno recuperar seus recursos mais rapidamente. O presidente afirmou na rede social X que os responsáveis por eventuais irregularidades deverão responder à Justiça, sem exceções.

articles.title: Sucuri gigante encontrada em Goiás já tinha comido gatos e galinhas, diz bombeiro  | G1
articles.standfirst: Serpente de aproximadamente 4,5 metros foi capturada quando tentava se alimentar de um cachorro, em Caldas Novas. Segundo tenente, animal já vinha atacando animais domésticos na região.
articles.summary: Serpente de aproximadamente 4,5 metros foi capturada quando tentava se alimentar de um cachorro, em Caldas Novas. Segundo tenente, animal já vinha atacando animais domésticos na região.
articles.body:
A sucuri-amarela de aproximadamente 4,5 metros capturada perto de uma residência no Setor Lagoa Quente, em Caldas Novas, no sul de Goiás, já havia se alimentado de galinhas e gatos que viviam na região . A informação foi confirmada ao g1 pelo tenente Fábio Mesquita, do Corpo de Bombeiros.

No dia da captura, na quarta-feira (4), a serpente estava prestes a devorar um cachorro que pertencia ao morador que acionou a equipe. Segundo o tenente, os moradores encontraram a sucuri com o cachorro e tentaram afastá-la. Com a movimentação, a serpente soltou o animal e se escondeu em um brejo próximo. Quando os bombeiros chegaram, o cachorro já estava morto, após ser asfixiado pela serpente.

A equipe retirou o corpo do cachorro do local e o colocou em uma área mais limpa. Os militares permaneceram nas proximidades e aguardaram. Quando a sucuri saiu do brejo e se aproximou novamente para se alimentar, os bombeiros conseguiram capturá-la.

“Ela pegou o cachorro, mas os moradores mexeram com ela e ela o soltou. Os bombeiros foram ao local e o colocou em uma área mais limpa. Ele já estava morto porque ela o asfixiou”, relatou o tenente.

O tenente explicou que a serpente foi levada ao Centro de Triagem e Reabilitação de Animais Silvestres (Cetras), em Caldas Novas. Depois, uma foto publicada pelo secretário municipal de Meio Ambiente, Sérgio Gustavo Silva, mostrou o animal sendo devolvido ao habitat natural .

A serpente foi capturada e levada ao Centro de Triagem e Reabilitação de Animais Silvestres pelo Corpo de Bombeiros — Foto: Divulgação/Corpo de Bombeiros

De acordo com Fábio Mesquita, cinco bombeiros participaram da captura. Ele contou que, em 20 anos de serviço na corporação em Caldas Novas, essa foi a terceira vez que participou de uma ocorrência envolvendo uma serpente desse porte.

“Mas nunca houve maior que essa. Ela é muito grande mesmo. Muito grande”, afirmou.

A sucuri foi encontrada em um ribeirão próximo à residência, no Setor Lagoa Quente. A presença do animal preocupou os moradores, principalmente pela circulação de crianças e de outros animais domésticos nas proximidades.

Ao g1 , o biólogo Edson Abrão explicou que a serpente é uma sucuri-amarela adulta. Pelas imagens, não foi possível identificar se o animal é macho ou fêmea. A espécie não possui peçonha, mas tem uma musculatura muito forte e captura suas presas por constrição.

“Então, ela não injeta peçonha quando morde uma pessoa. Mas ela mata animais por constrição, ela é um animal muito forte. Na América do Sul, ela é a serpente que mais tem força no corpo, e se alimenta de qualquer animal”, explicou.

🔍 A constrição é uma forma de predação em que a serpente envolve o corpo da presa e usa a força muscular para imobilizá-la. A alimentação da sucuri pode incluir mamíferos, peixes, jacarés e até outras serpentes.

Segundo Abrão, por ser semiaquática, a sucuri pode ter se aproximado da residência em busca de abrigo ou alimento. Ele também destacou que a presença de um animal adulto e desse porte na região pode indicar equilíbrio ecológico.

O biólogo ressaltou que a espécie ocupa uma posição importante na cadeia alimentar, ajudando a controlar populações de outros animais. Ele reforçou ainda que serpentes não devem ser mortas quando aparecem em áreas residenciais.

O Corpo de Bombeiros orienta que, ao encontrar uma serpente, a população mantenha distância e não tente tocar, capturar ou afugentar o animal. Crianças e animais domésticos devem ser afastados do local.

Se possível, o animal pode ser observado de longe, sem ser cercado ou acuado. Para solicitar atendimento especializado, a orientação é acionar o Corpo de Bombeiros pelo telefone 193 .

*Michely Loures é integrante do programa de estágio entre TV Anhanguera e Universidade Federal de Goiás (UFG), sob orientação de Gilmara Roberto.

articles.summary: A proposta aprovada em Idaho escolheu o Winchester 1873, modelo do século 19 conhecido como 'a arma que conquistou o Oeste' e símbolo da expansão americana.
articles.body:
Rifle Winchester modelo 1873. — Foto: Reprodução

Além de decidir novos representantes na Câmara e no Senado, as eleições de meio de mandato dos Estados Unidos , conhecida como midterms, parte do país também teve que votar em propostas estaduais. Uma delas foi a aprovação da arma oficial do estado de Idaho.

O armamento escolhido foi o Rifle Winchester modelo 1873 , conhecida mundialmente como a arma do filme de faroeste "A Conquista do Oeste" .

O modelo foi desenvolvido no século 19 e ficou conhecido pelo apelido de "a arma que conquistou o Oeste", em referência à sua popularidade durante a expansão dos Estados Unidos para o oeste do território. O rifle se tornou um dos símbolos da cultura dos filmes de faroeste, gênero marcado por histórias de caubóis, duelos e expansão territorial.

Com a aprovação da proposta, Idaho passa a ter uma arma oficial, assim como outros estados americanos que adotaram símbolos próprios para representar sua história e cultura.

No Idaho tiveram que escolher qual seria a arma oficial do estado. — Foto: Reprodução/X

articles.title: Pope Leo heads to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Pope Leo, who had part of a lung removed last month, will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".

It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.

At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".

"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.

"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."

The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.

The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.

Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.

"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.

"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"

The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.

This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.

But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.

The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.

"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.

Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.

His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.

He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.

In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.

"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.

He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.

"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

articles.title: 'I was asked if I was a crier': Your worst job interviews revealed
articles.summary: Bad job interviews can be horrible to experience in the moment, but there is a lot they can teach us about the world of work
articles.body:
Tiara Allen arrived on time to interview for a retail job. Her interviewer didn't.

She waited for around 40 minutes in a shopping centre while the interviewer's co-worker called them "two or three times".

When they finally showed up, Tiara says she was told it was because the meeting wasn't in the schedule.

She needed work at the time, so took the job when she was offered it, but says she would handle the situation differently now.

"I would not take a job if they took that long," she says, adding that she believed her treatment during the interview was a sign of how the firm tended to treat staff.

Tiara is far from alone. She is one of many people who spoke to the BBC about their worst job interview experiences after we wrote about the one interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable .

While those situations can be hard to deal with in the moment, they can also teach us a lot about the world of work.

During an interview for an assistant at a book publisher in New York, Chas Edwards was asked a question he wasn't expecting.

"I was asked for my first job if I was a crier," he recalls.

Thinking the interviewer was being funny, Chas replied that he didn't cry. He was later told that this was why he got the job.

"Her last assistant had cried – too often, I guess? – and she wanted someone who didn't cry. So she was being serious and I thought it was a joke," he says.

It was a bad sign. Chas says it was "a terrible, terrible job with a miserable boss" and while he managed to make it through 13 months there without crying he was "crying inside".

"I set the world record for working for this person. No-one had ever lasted three months with her before," he recalls.

Despite all this, Chas says he is in some ways grateful the experience was so awful.

"Because every job since then, even the bad ones, are not that bad," he says, adding that he can "cry anywhere now".

Corinne Card also found herself floored when the first question she was asked in an interview for an administrative job was if she liked working with people.

When she replied yes, she was told that the job wouldn't be for her and the interview ended there.

"I don't know if it was a deliberate trap. Because who would answer 'I don't like working with people'?"

Corinne Mills, joint managing director of Personal Career Management, says that it can be worth asking an interviewer to clarify any weird questions, perhaps by repeating the question back to them.

However, if a line of questioning is really off-putting, she says it can also be a sign of what it's like to work there, saying that interviews are also about candidates judging the company.

Meanwhile, other questions are not just annoying – they are illegal.

Discrimination against a protected characteristic is against the law , meaning an employer cannot treat you less favourably based on your age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation.

Employment lawyer Roy Magara says that women being asked if they intend on having children in an interview is a "quite common" kind of bias. He says he has also seen a case where an older candidate was told he didn't get the job after an interview because he didn't fit the "vibe" of a younger team.

If you think these sorts of biases took place in your interview, Roy says you can send the company a subject access request to see how they discussed your application internally.

Worst-case scenarios like these can make interviews feel very difficult, especially considering the control employers have over candidates.

Euan Cameron, co-founder of hiring software Willo, says that even with this power imbalance it's important not to overthink what an interview is.

"An interview is just a conversation between two people," he says.

Of course, as in Tiara's case, it helps when both of those people show up.

articles.title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'
articles.summary: Investment has surged into the making of jet turbine blades - an extremely difficult component to make.
articles.body:
Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines.

Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C.

It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown.

During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification.

Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes.

"It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning."

Only a handful of companies around the world can produce these single crystal turbine blades, and the process has been perfected end-to-end in just five countries, including the US and UK. Engine-makers continually vie for access to the technology.

Rolls-Royce, GE and France's Safran are among the few firms that have perfected the process.

In September, GE Aerospace announced it would acquire its turbine blade supplier for $11.75bn (£8.78bn). Neither company responded to BBC News' requests for comment but the move has been described as an effort to ensure supply of these critical components.

Separately, in March, Rolls-Royce said it would invest more than £19m in its Rotherham blade casting facility.

Turbine blade specialists continue to work on improving the capabilities of this little-known technology. All the while, China is desperate to prove that its engineers can produce turbine blades of the same quality as those in the West. Who will come out on top?

"Demand for [turbine blades] is huge. So few companies have managed to do it, which does give it this kind of magical aura," says Bill Sweetman, an aviation industry writer and consultant.

He suspects GE Aerospace's recent move is about securing reliability and predictability in the notoriously volatile aircraft manufacturing supply chain.

But why is the single crystal casting process, which has been around for decades now, still so specialist?

To grow one of these blades, asserts Fifoot, is to "fight the laws of the universe".

This is because each molten blade would naturally cool into a solid object consisting of many small grains of metal alloy, all jumbled together. But you don't want a crumbly sugar cube, you want a perfect diamond.

Getting a single crystal to grow into the shape of the blade instead isn't just a matter of cooling the molten version down slowly, the process also uses a bizarre trick called a pigtail.

The pigtail is a small spiral at one end of the blade. Fifoot says that, at the beginning of the cooling process, this spiral "chokes" the flow of solidifying crystals so that just one takes over. A bit like a hairpin corner in an F1 race right before the finish line – one driver can take the lead here and go on to win.

"Sometimes we need to play around with the number of turns or the angles on [the pigtail] to try and get more favourable grain," adds Fifoot. Once the blade is formed, this crucial but sacrificial spiral is cut off.

Blades made by Rolls-Royce are used in aircraft engines including the Trent XWB-84, which powers the Airbus A350-900, and the Trent 1000 XE, for the Boeing 787.

The single crystal is essential to ensure each blade's performance. Sometimes a blade doesn't cool quite as planned, for example two crystals form within it instead of just one, and the metal alloy must be reprocessed so that the manufacturer may re-use the material.

Special ceramic coatings also protect blades from extreme temperatures inside engines. And another important feature is that blades are cast with tiny channels that allow a flow of cooler air to coat them in a kind of film while the aircraft engine is working.

"The drive at the moment [across the industry] is currently to make those cooling passages really intricate," says Paul Withey, at the University of Birmingham, who formerly worked for Rolls-Royce. The more turbulent those little flows of cool air are, he explains, the more they will knock heat out of the surrounding, much hotter air.

And blade-makers also seek to reduce the mass of these components as much as possible.

"If we can take any weight out of it, you can run that engine more efficiently using less fuel – you can spin it faster and hotter," says Fifoot.

Meanwhile, China hopes to become only the sixth country to master the whole technology chain for single crystal blade casting.

A report in May quoted one engineer at the AECC Beijing Institute of Aeronautical Materials claiming that China now had a single crystal alloy "superior to or equivalent to the second-generation single-crystal superalloys widely used in Europe and the US". It costs less to make, too, apparently.

But the West has a "huge advantage" over China given that the majority of commercial airliner production happens there, says Sweetman. Supply chains and the latest innovations are generally clustered in the West. Plus, Western manufacturers also have lengthy safety records under their belts.

China must compete on practically every aspect of aircraft manufacturing – by no means just on turbine blades – in order to make serious in-roads. "You can definitely see that happening but it's a long, uphill struggle," adds Sweetman.

Demand for aircraft is currently high, which is already straining various supply chains in the industry. That demand could grow higher still, suggests Withey.

During the next few years, one of the two main aircraft manufacturers, Airbus and Boeing, could launch a new short-haul plane , he says. Then, the other would have to follow suit in order to remain competitive.

"There'll be a bun fight," says Withey, over who gets to supply the engines and, by extension, those all-important single crystal turbine blades.

articles.title: Turkiye’s parliament ratifies Mecca defence agreement
articles.summary: Parliament’s approval lays the groundwork for further Turkish involvement in Saudi Arabia’s conflict with the Houthis.
articles.body:
Turkiye’s parliament has ratified a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that includes a collective defence clause, committing NATO’s second-largest military to the group’s aid in case of attack.

The ratification on Thursday comes as Riyadh continues to face attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.

Turkiye first signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August and sent it to parliament for ratification last month.

Article 1 of a bill approving the pact was adopted by the Turkish parliament on Wednesday.

But afterwards, Deputy Parliament Speaker Celal Adan adjourned the session until Thursday afternoon, the Anadolu news agency reported.

After parliament returned to session, lawmakers continued to debate the other articles in the pact.

The agreement ultimately passed with 279 votes in favour and 119 against, with 398 of the chamber’s 592 lawmakers taking part in the vote.

The pact contains 16 articles, according to a document submitted to the Turkish parliament, seen by the Reuters news agency.

In Article 1 of the accord, the signatories shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity. Article 1 can be invoked in case of an attack on any member state.

Once the first article is invoked, the document lays out provisions for what follows.

“In the event one of the parties is subjected to an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the parties shall immediately provide assistance to the party under attack, utilising the full range of mutual assistance measures available to them,” says Article 2 of the pact.

This key clause mirrors Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, the document that established the NATO military alliance. NATO’s Article 5 establishes that an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

Given that Turkiye is a member of both NATO and the Mecca pact, critics have raised questions about whether the country’s government might face a conflict of interest in allocating its military resources.

Turkish officials, however, have dismissed such concerns as unfounded.

Other articles in the Mecca pact concern a mutual agreement to increase defence industry cooperation and military coordination, with the aim of deterring threats.

Those articles, in part, commit member states to conducting joint training, pursuing technological innovation and sharing logistics and intelligence resources.

The draft approved by Turkish lawmakers commits member countries to the pact for 10 years, after which point they may withdraw.

It also leaves open the possibility of other countries joining, with the approval of the pact’s existing members. Syria’s government has already expressed interest .

Despite Thursday’s parliamentary ratification, it is not a foregone conclusion that Turkish troops would be deployed to Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks.

Experts say any Turkish troop deployment would also require other legislative processes.

Turkiye’s Defence Minister Yasar Guler said in October that the scope of potential support for Saudi Arabia would be determined after ratification.

“We absolutely do not foresee entering into any conflict with the Houthis,” Turkish media reported Guler as saying. Instead, Turkish support “would be to strengthen deterrence”.

Tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen had abated somewhat following a 2022 ceasefire. But the Houthis have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent months, notably launching a series of deadly strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

The region also remains embroiled in the US-Israel war on Iran, which has contributed to cross-border tensions.

On Thursday, Saudi Arabia announced it had intercepted a drone in the region of Medina. Riyadh has accused the Houthis several times of targeting Mecca and Medina, two holy cities in Islam, an accusation the Iran-backed group systematically rejects.

articles.title: Salon, an early staple of internet discourse, announces it will shut down
articles.summary: “It has been an extraordinary privilege,” the outlet, which for 31 years published sharp voices and political and cultural journalism backed by a liberal sensibility, said in a farewell note.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Salon, one of the early internet's most influential websites that featured sharp voices and political and cultural journalism backed by a liberal sensibility, announced Thursday it would shut down after 31 years of publication. “It has been an extraordinary privilege,” the outlet said in a farewell note. The announcement, seen as a surprise, cited the fact that “the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years.” It did not immediately indicate what would become of its employees, though some reported they had lost their jobs. “Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own,” the unsigned farewell note said. “Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives.” It began shortly after the internet went big Salon began its life in the mid-1990s, barely three years after the internet itself went mainstream and a time when the “World Wide Web” was still written out in that fashion. It launched a decade before the newspaper and print magazine markets imploded — and a decade, too, before the rise of social media fragmented the journalism world. As its name suggested, Salon was initially styled as an online magazine and meeting place, a site where more provocative opinions and stories that might not be at home in daily newspapers or even then-dominant newsweeklies like Time or Newsweek could surface and generate discussion. It quickly became a place where writers wanted their work to appear. “The timing was right — readers were tired of bland, market-tested media products, and the internet allowed us to launch something original, something with a strong voice,” founder David Talbot said on the outlet’s fifth anniversary in 2000. It drew a cadre of high-profile writers and people who would become famous, including Jake Tapper and Glenn Greenwald. Two of its editors-in-chief, Talbot and Joan Walsh, went on to become prominent progressive political voices as well. As the internet grew, so did Salon's competition. Slate emerged the following year, and soon after, online magazines became the order of the day. Eventually, older print publications like The Atlantic began putting more content online, and the marketplace of online ideas grew. Salon used Princess Diana's death in 1997 to go beyond its culture-and-criticism roots and wade into breaking news coverage. No word on what becomes of its content Salon did not immediately say what would become of its immense online archives, which include three decades of stories from across the world and across topics and genres. In the statement, Salon also made a point of thanking its readers. “You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered,” it said. “You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.”

articles.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor received up to £2,000 per month from sub-letting, watchdog reports
articles.summary: The income went to the former prince rather than his landlord the Crown Estate.
articles.body:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was receiving up to £2,000 per month for sub-letting three cottages at his former home at Royal Lodge, when he didn't have to pay any rent himself, according to the public spending watchdog.

The Public Accounts Committee inquiry into the Crown Estate says the former Prince Andrew did not always rent out all the properties, so it cannot say how much the total might have been over more than 20 years of his time there.

The sub-letting income went to Mountbatten-Windsor, rather than his landlord the Crown Estate.

MPs on the committee have recommended that in future such leases should prohibit sub-letting, unless specifically agreed with the landlord.

He has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein and has been approached for comment.

The Public Accounts Committee has examined the leases on such royal properties as part of a wider inquiry into the management of the Crown Estate, which is an independent property company that pays its profits to the Treasury.

Mountbatten-Windsor had taken on a 75-year lease for Royal Lodge in 2003 and had paid about £7.5m towards its renovation and other charges, which meant that he did not have to pay rent.

But it emerged that as a tenant he had been intermittently sub-letting three cottages that were part of the property, which was thought to be for staff and at a below market rate, with Mountbatten-Windsor keeping the income.

The Crown Estate had told MPs that it did not have any oversight over how much Mountbatten-Windsor charged - and sub-letting was allowed as part of his lease.

But the MPs have recommended that in future the default position for such Crown Estate properties should be that such sub-letting should be banned, unless there was a specific exemption.

The Public Accounts Committee report also confirms what has happened since Mountbatten-Windsor's departure from Royal Lodge.

There was a payment of about £300,000 due to him for his early surrender of his lease, but because of "dilapidations" in the state of the building, there was a repair bill of £1.8m.

That meant the Crown Estate was owed £1.5m, which King Charles paid on his brother's behalf.

The watchdog's report also highlighted concerns about the level of rent being charged to non-working royals who had been given accommodation in three royal properties.

That was believed to be Mountbatten-Windsor's daughters, Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie, and Prince and Princess Michael of Kent.

A National Audit Office report had revealed earlier this year that Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie do not pay anything themselves for their accommodation in St James's Palace and Kensington Palace respectively.

The King pays their rent to the Royal Household from his own private income.

But the group of MPs were concerned about whether the level of rent on such properties for non-working royals was based on up-to-date valuations and recommended a more consistent approach to ensure value for money.

There was criticism too for the Crown Estate concentrating too much of its urban property portfolio in London and the south east of England, with MPs calling for more of a regional spread.

There were also warnings about how the Crown Estate's administration costs had increased significantly, at a time when MPs noted government budgets were under pressure.

The report said administration costs had risen by 129% since 2020-21 and that the chief executive, Dan Labbad's salary had risen by 106% over that time. In 2025-26 his pay package was worth £2.3m.

In response, a Crown Estate spokeswoman said: "The Public Accounts Committee report is an important part of our accountability to Parliament. We are considering its findings and recommendations and will respond to the Committee in due course."

articles.title: Are you an evening snacker? What you need to know
articles.summary: There are biological reasons why you may reach for sweet treats before bed, but you can change the habit.
articles.body:
You've eaten dinner, you're comfortably full, and yet half an hour later you're raiding the kitchen cupboards. Sound familiar?

Research suggests about a third of people are snacking every night after their evening meal - for those aged 18-24, four in five are unable to resist.

Dietitian Dr Kristine Beaulieu says this spells trouble. She points to evidence showing that the more people eat within two hours of going to bed, the "greater the odds" of weight gain and obesity.

So, why are evening cravings so common? And what can you do to keep them in check?

Despite the fact we spend longer going without food when we are sleeping, research suggests our appetite naturally peaks in the evening, almost regardless of how much we have eaten earlier in the day.

Prof James Betts, who researches how the body handles food and energy at the University of Bath, says a big factor is that our "hunger hormone" ghrelin is generally higher later in the day.

"While it tends to be suppressed by meals, that really only happens after the first meal of the day, not after lunch or dinner."

But what you eat also matters. Meals rich in protein, fibre and volume tend to keep us satisfied for longer.

Betts says not having a nutritious or satiating evening meal can lead to a "crash" later, which sees people snack.

For others, the fear of waking up hungry during the night is also a motivating factor, while habit plays a role too.

"If snacking often happens in the same setting, the surrounding cues can start to trigger cravings," says Prof Suzanne Higgs, an expert in appetite at the University of Birmingham.

"For example, if someone usually snacks while watching TV, simply turning the TV on may make them feel like eating."

It's not just feelings of hunger that increase later in the day. Research suggests our appetite for calorie-dense foods also becomes stronger, driven by the brain's reward system rather than a genuine need for energy.

"Our liking and wanting for high-fat foods are greater later in the day compared to low-fat foods," says Beaulieu, who splits her time between the University of Leeds and University of Moncton in Canada.

"That hedonic drive can override signals of fullness, making us want to snack or eat a dessert even though we're full."

Even after a substantial evening meal, foods rich in sugar, fat or salt can continue to activate reward pathways in the brain, helping explain why many people find themselves reaching for something more.

So when you find yourself standing in front of the biscuit tin at 9pm, it may not be a lack of willpower. Your biology is stacked against you.

The evidence is mixed. But certainly eating a large meal late affects digestion and the body's normal preparation for sleep.

What about snacking? Here the research becomes less clear.

There is some evidence that foods high in refined carbohydrates and added sugars, from white bread and white rice to biscuits and cakes, may be linked to poorer sleep.

Researchers think this could be because such foods cause bigger swings in blood sugar levels and may alter some of the hormonal signals involved in regulating sleep and appetite.

However, teasing out cause and effect is difficult. People with poor sleep may be more likely to snack on sugary foods.

"Sleep deprivation is known to not only increase appetite, but also a desire for energy-dense foods," says Prof Jonathan Johnston, a sleep and body clock expert at the University of Surrey.

It means it is very difficult to draw firm conclusions on whether snacking in late evening disrupts sleep, says Betts.

"The evidence is far from clear and perhaps may reflect that some people respond differently to others to different foods before bed."

First, work out what's driving the snacking.

If you are genuinely hungry, it may help to make earlier meals more filling

If snacking is mainly habitual, changing routines and planning snacks in advance can help

"Eating while distracted, for instance watching TV, can lead people to consume more because they pay less attention to how much they've eaten," says Higgs.

But there's no need to ban evening snacks completely, says Beaulieu.

A reasonable portion of something enjoyable is often more sustainable

Keep healthy options, such as fruit, yoghurt and nuts available

Even a little chocolate every now and then is not the end of the world

"It's OK to eat those craved foods once in a while in moderation."

The trick, she says, is to make the healthy choice the default.

"If those craved foods aren't in the cupboard on a regular basis and a healthy option is, it means you are more likely to choose the healthier option."

articles.title: U2 on Dolly Parton's final duet; and the 'grudge match' behind their new album
articles.summary: The rock group discuss Parton's final recording before her death, and why they refuse to be censored on stage.
articles.body:
U2 are at their best when they act on instinct.

Their biggest songs are fuelled by fiery indignation (Pride, Sunday Bloody Sunday) or sudden inspiration (One, Sometimes You Can't Make It On Your Own).

When they overthink, they misfire. An attempt to marry grunge and hip-hop on the 2006 single Get On Your Boots was, in the words of drummer Larry Mullen Jr, "a catastrophic choice".

So it was a good sign when, at the start of 2026, the band rushed out two EPs of new music, ripped from the headlines of a world in turmoil.

The first, Days of Ash, was urgent and angry – addressing the shooting of US citizen Renee Good by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer; and the death of Palestinian activist Odeh Hathaleenm, who was allegedly killed by an Israeli settler. Yinon Levy has been charged with reckless manslaughter and said he would fight for his innocence in court.

U2's follow-up, Easter Lily, was more reflective, asking whether faith and friendship are enough to sustain us in challenging times.

Together, they were the band's strongest material in years, combining the combustive power of their early, post-punk incarnation with the melodic sophistication they developed in the late 1980s.

"We put those EPs out without telling anyone," says Bono, the band's voluble frontman.

"Our management, our label, they all said, 'You can't do that, people won't notice'.

"And we said, 'We don't mind. It's okay not to have a big hype behind everything'.

"And it was really beautiful. The people who we wanted to notice, noticed."

For long-term U2 watchers, that's a big shift.

This is the group who described their 2000 album All That You Can't Leave Behind as the sound of four men "re-applying for the job of biggest band in the world"; and who forced 2014's Songs of Innocence into 500 million people's iTunes libraries - an epic act of overreach that Bono's been apologising for ever since .

There's no such hoopla around their new album, Carnaval de Luz, which is getting a pretty traditional roll-out for one of the world's biggest rock bands.

Sure, there's the requisite deluge of box sets and vinyl variants, a filmed concert for BBC Two , and a handful of interviews, including this one. But, more than ever, U2 want the music to speak for itself.

The album's a companion piece and a counterbalance to Days of Ash and Easter Lily. Inspired by ecstatic nights at music festivals, it rejects anxiety in favour of what Bono calls "defiant joy".

There's a stirring ballad titled If The World Is at War, We Better Not Be; while the chiming guitars of Superficiality lend an optimism to Bono's affirmation that, "the news can't break us".

"We didn't want to be dragged down by dark clouds or melancholy," explains bassist Adam Clayton.

"Our journey from the mid 1970s was about expanding freedom and opportunity for everyone: Make your own rules, pull down what wasn't useful. Now we seem to be in a period where that's under threat and under attack.

"We wanted to make the point that we didn't want our joy robbed."

During recording sessions last year, Bono told me U2 were chasing " the sound of the future ". In a separate interview with Radio 2's Jo Whiley, guitarist The Edge claimed they were working on an album of " sci-fi Irish folk" .

The electronic groove of the opening track, Go (Carnaval de Luz), echoes their experimental 90s phase; while the serrated riffs of Silencio are direct descendants of 2004's Vertigo.

U2 celebrate 50th anniversary at the school where they formed

The sci-fi folk idea persists, however, on the closing track Torn – a duet with Dolly Parton, that became the country star's last ever recording.

To court the first lady of country, Bono sent her a set of bagpipes for her birthday. Intrigued, she agreed to listen to his demos.

"We had some folk songs we were playing, there was one called Lifelong, and I remember her saying, 'You know, that's a little too Irish for me'," he recalls.

"So she said, 'Look, I've started a song called Torn. You can take it where you want, and I might like where you take it'.

Parton's original lyric was about a woman trying to choose between two men but, with help from Snow Patrol's Jonny McDaid, U2 rewrote the song to address the political divisions tearing families apart.

" Brothers turn to strangers /And sons deny their name / Somebody loses either way And every heart is torn ."

Parton recorded her parts in June, less than three months before she died.

"We knew she was ill, but we had no idea that it'd be her last vocal," says Bono.

"That was a real shock. A shock for us because we'd been working with her, but a shock for anyone who loves music.

"I remember I was with [R.E.M. frontman] Michael Stipe in a car when the news came in, and he actually fell down and started sobbing. He just could not believe it.

"Probably the only thing that people can agree on in the entire world right now is Dolly Parton. Whether you're gay or straight or conservative or liberal, she was ready for you to fly at her show."

Another female presence shimmers on the fourth track, The Mirror Maker, which is dedicated to Catalan superstar Rosalía. Written after witnessing her spell-binding Lux tour , Bono describes the "heavens swirling" to reveal "the re-enchantment of the world".

"Normally you have to be dead or in jail for us to write a song about you," he laughs, "but she's a feminine force field. A kind of transcendent, ecstatic musician."

He wrote the song without her knowledge, phoning the singer afterwards to timidly seek her approval.

"It could have been excruciating if she really, really hated it," he grimaces. "I'd have had to pretend it was about Santa Rosalia, a saint who lived in a cave in Italy in the 17th Century."

According to producer Jacknife Lee, The Mirror Maker went through 196 different takes before U2 were happy, suggesting they haven't entirely abandoned their perfectionist streak.

"The early sessions for this album were at times super inspiring, and then really not that good at all," admits The Edge, identifying a stubborn "stick-with-it-ness" that stops them from giving up.

"This band is absolutely relentless," agrees Bono. "It's a grudge match."

"It's the most frustrating thing," Mullen Jr adds. "I'm always reminded of how incapable I am of doing all those things that other people find easy.

"It's always been a challenge for us, and that's what makes those moments when it [works] so special. That's why you keep on chasing it, and why you stay in a band."

There's more to U2's longevity than that, though. Their line-up has remained unchanged since they first formed at Dublin's Mount Temple Comprehensive School 50 years ago. They remain friends first, and superstars second.

When we meet, in a bingo hall that hosted some of U2's formative gigs, there's a familial vibe to the whole operation.

They tease Mullen Jr for turning a hose on fans who climbed the wall of his parents' house in 1976; and chat animatedly about their musical obsessions ("every four-piece wants to be the Beatles," confesses Bono).

Those bonds have kept the band together through commercial and critical ups and downs, not to mention the life-altering injuries that forced Bono to cancel a 2010 US tour, and neck problems that prompted Mullen Jr to skip their 2023-2024 Las Vegas residency.

Doctors advised him to retire, but after a (risky) surgical intervention, he's back behind the kit – developing an entirely new playing style to avoid further damage.

His determination will be put to the test next year, when U2 embark on a massive international stadium tour, including two UK dates at London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium next June.

The US leg will see them play some of the same venues as their friend, Ed Sheeran. So what did they make of the controversy over his recent US tour – where some venue owners pressured Sheeran into dropping his support act, Macklemore, for making pro-Palestinian comments?

"We totally support Macklemore's right as an artist to say what he wanted to say," says The Edge.

"I don't think Ed should be vilified. He was in a very difficult situation. But I commend the other young artists who decided to leave [his] tour.

"They were sticking up for an artist's right to free speech, and I think that's the issue above anything else."

He recalls several occasions where U2 themselves made risky political statements on stage.

In 1987, after Arizona's governor banned Martin Luther King Day, Bono faced death threats if he dared to play Pride (In The Name of Love) - which addresses King's assassination - in the state.

He went ahead and did it anyway, closing his eyes in anticipation of a gunshot.

"I looked up at the end of the verse and I clearly wasn't dead," he later told Mojo magazine. 'But not only that... Adam Clayton was standing in front of me."

Similarly, in 1998, the band taunted Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet during a televised concert in Santiago. At the end of the night, they invited the mothers of the victims of Pinochet's 1973 coup d'état on to the stage, who took it in turns to say the names of their children into the microphone.

"It would have been way smarter and better for us to shut up," says the Edge. "But it was artistically necessary, and we just said, 'We can't not do this'."

Reflecting further on the Macklemore controversy, he adds: "We might disagree with some of the members of the pro-Palestine movement, but we absolutely agree with the fundamentals. We absolutely agree that what's going on [in Gaza] is unconscionable and that a child's life is equally valuable, no matter what their background."

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Mullen Jr is equally forthright about the freedom to speak out.

"We, as a band, will fight for the right to speak your mind, as long as it doesn't incite violence," he says.

"Even if we disagree with it or don't like it, nobody - no billionaire, no promoter, no owner - has the right to censor anybody.

"And they will definitely not be censoring us, ever."

Like I said: U2 are at their best when they trust their instincts.

articles.title: Sir Mark Rowley: Policing is 'heading for failure' without reform
articles.summary: Sir Mark Rowley will argue that the current system is unable to cope with the sophistication of modern criminals.
articles.body:
The head of the Metropolitan Police is to warn that policing in England and Wales is "heading for failure" without urgent reform.

In a speech on Friday, Sir Mark Rowley will call for the system to change, arguing it is unable to cope with the sophistication of modern criminals.

He is proposing eight to 10 regional police forces, supported by hundreds of local policing commands and a new National Police Service, in what would be the biggest overhaul since the 1960s.

The changes would replace the 43-force structure with three tiers: local teams dealing with neighbourhood issues, regional forces sharing specialist resources and a National Police Service tackling the most serious crimes.

Sir Mark says organised crime groups, fraud networks, cyber-criminals and those involved in online child abuse increasingly operate across regional and international borders, while police forces remain organised around local areas.

He will warn that the current system is struggling to keep pace with these threats, saying: "We have 43 overstretched forces trying to do too much, with too little."

He believes merging forces would reduce duplication, arguing this could free up thousands of roles to be redirected towards front line policing.

His proposals follow a consultation launched by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood in January. This included plans for a National Police Service to tackle the most complex crimes and a possible merger of the 43 forces into fewer, larger forces.

However some rural police and crime commissioners have described the plans as "political manoeuvring" by larger forces to "load the dice in their favour".

The Association of Police and Crime Commissioners (APCC) has also questioned whether merging forces is the best way to improve policing.

It said: "The case for modernisation and a National Police Service is clear. The case for reducing 43 forces to nine regional 'mega-forces' is not."

A Home Office spokesperson defended the plans, saying: "Our current model of policing has not changed since the 1960s and is no longer fit for purpose."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has not yet commented.

Sir Mark has also highlighted the financial pressures facing policing, asserting that spending on policing had fallen from about 0.9% of GDP to 0.7% since 2010.

He says years of underinvestment have left forces relying on ageing technology, while officers are increasingly diverted from neighbourhood policing to deal with other demands, including mental health and social care.

He will also point to falling police performance, saying positive outcomes nationally are now less than half the level they were 12 years ago, while public confidence has fallen by 9%.

articles.title: Could the earliest weakening of the polar vortex on record bring UK snow?
articles.summary: An unprecedented early weakening of the polar vortex is causing uncertainty amongst experts over the impact it will have on UK weather as Simon King explains.
articles.body:
High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.

But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.

While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.

Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.

However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.

The polar vortex develops every autumn as temperatures fall in the Arctic.

Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface, locking the coldest air near the pole.

Atmospheric disturbances can cause the air high up to start warming which then makes the vortex winds weaken. This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.

In the following days and weeks these changes can alter the position of the jet stream, increasing the chance of a blocked weather pattern where it can become drier with a colder northerly or easterly wind bringing Arctic air in.

It can also boost the possibility of snow, especially in eastern UK.

Most SSW events tend to occur from mid-winter but we are currently witnessing a dramatic weakening of the strong winds with some forecasts even showing a reversal of the polar vortex winds by mid-November.

Due to this weakening, the vortex has stretched and briefly split into two smaller circulations around the Arctic.

If the winds continue to weaken and end up reversing as forecast, this will be known as a major SSW event.

Jeff Knight, lead climate scientist from the Met Office, told the BBC: "It would appear to be the earliest on record looking back over the 75 years we've been observing…with most experts agreeing this is a very unusual event."

The current earliest major SSW event occurred on 28 November in 1969 and 2025.

Reasons for why we're seeing such an early event is not clear. It could be just part of the variability of our weather patterns.

But we also know in a "normal" El Niño year, this can typically bring a weakening of the polar vortex towards the end of winter.

While the warmer waters of the Pacific in an El Niño directly disrupt the weather around tropical areas, pulses of energy in the atmosphere, known as planetary waves, can cause disturbances even at polar regions.

These waves can push the polar vortex out of position and break the circulation up.

With the current record El Niño taking us into uncharted territory in terms of disruption to worldwide weather patterns, Knight suggested it could have "helped load the dice for this SSW event. However, because this is so rare, there's not enough evidence".

A link between a strong El Niño and early onset of a SSW event is unclear and will need further research.

Long-range forecasts issued by the Met Office show that the UK was more likely to see a stormy start to winter, followed by a colder spell to end winter. This is consistent with expectations from an El Niño pattern.

However, this unusually early SSW event was not widely expected.

Professor Andrew Perez-Charlton, meteorologist at the University of Reading, said: "The typical response to a SSW is for colder and drier conditions over Europe and the UK."

"Because we haven't seen a SSW event quite like this before, it is harder to anticipate a cold spell at the moment."

The Arctic is not yet as cold as it becomes later in winter, with the polar vortex itself having only recently developed.

Any influence it may have on weather patterns could be weaker than during a mid-winter disruption.

And because the air isn't at mid-winter temperatures yet it means cold and snowy weather for the UK is far from guaranteed.

Continuation of drought conditions "more concerning"

Long-term forecasts are based on large-scale climate signals and how they have affected weather patterns in previous years.

Much of the forecast for this autumn and winter has been focused around the influence of the exceptionally strong El Niño, pointing to a stormier start to winter, with the potential to be followed by colder and drier conditions from January.

But this unusually early disruption of the polar vortex and SSW presents meteorologists with a situation for which there are few modern comparisons.

For Perez-Charlton, the "concerning thing would be if this event ends up bringing the typical drier weather pattern and lack of rain" associated with a sudden stratospheric warming over the coming months.

With most of England and Wales still in drought, we need to rely on a wetter winter to fill up extremely low reservoirs.

For now, experts stress that it is too early to know whether recent changes in the polar vortex will change the winter outlook.
